During the period of counting the Omer, certain mourning rituals are observed: one does not cut one's hair, shave, listen to music, or hold weddings and other parties. Some permit shaving during this period. These practices commemorate a plague that killed twelve thousand pairs of students of Rabbi Akiva who, the Talmud says, did not honor one another properly. The Ashkenazi community intensified these mourning customs in the wake of the pogroms of the First Crusade, which took place in Iyar and Sivan in the year 1096 (4856).

parts.text: 279 When Shavuot eve falls on Friday night,
parts.en: When Shavuot eve falls on Friday night, Ma'ariv is preceded by the last two psalms of Kabbalat Shabbat: Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat and Adonai Malach. Bameh Madlikin is omitted. VeShamru and the special verse for Yom Tov (Vayidaber Moshe) precede the Yom Tov Amida, which is said with additions for Shabbat. After the Amida, the congregation says Vayechulu, and the Shaliaḥ Tzibbur says the abbreviated Repetition of the Amida as is customary on Shabbat eve. When Shavuot eve falls on Motza'ei Shabbat, the congregation adds the paragraph Vatodi'enu in the middle section of the Amida. Similarly, in Kiddush, the two blessings for Havdala are inserted prior to the blessing Shehecheyanu; thus the order of blessings is: wine, Kiddush, flame, Havdala, Shehecheyanu.

en:Gates to Prayer/Guide to the Jewish Y.en: From the 17th of Tammuz until Tisha B'Av (the 'Three Weeks'), certain mourning rituals are observed: one does not cut one's hair, shave, listen to music, buy new things, or hold weddings and other parties. Some permit shaving during this period.

From Rosh Chodesh Av through Tisha B'Av (the 'Nine Days') additional mourning rituals are observed: one abstains from eating meat or drinking wine, clothes are not laundered or pressed, and one generally minimizes joyful activities.

parts.en: Shabbat Chazon (Shabbat preceding Tisha B'Av). The Shabbat preceding Tisha B'Av is known as Shabbat Chazon, named for the first word of the Haftara, Chazon. On Friday night, many congregations sing Lekha Dodi to the melody of Eli Tzion. The special Haftara (Is. 1:1–27) is read to the tune of Eikha.

According to the Mishna (Ta'anit 4:6), the fast of the 9th of Av commemorates five calamities that befell the Jewish people on that date: (1) God decreed that the children of Israel would not be allowed to enter the land of Israel, (2) the First Temple was destroyed, (3) the Second Temple was destroyed, (4) Beitar was captured, and (5) Jerusalem was plowed over.

parts.text: 309 During the silent recitation of the Amida (page 211),
parts.en: During the silent recitation of the Amida, the congregation says Nachem as part of the fourteenth blessing (Boneh Yerushalayim), Aneinu as part of the sixteenth blessing (Shomea Tefilla) (unless one is not fasting), and Sim Shalom in place of Shalom Rav. Mincha ends with Full Kaddish and Aleinu.

139 Torah Reading: pages 1161–1167. The Torah reading is repeated,
parts.en: Torah Reading: pages 1161–1167. The Torah reading is repeated, in cycles of five aliyot, until all males over thirteen have received an aliya [Rema Orach Chaim 697:1]. It is customary for children under 13 years to participate in an aliya, known as Kol HaNe'arim, in which multiple tallitot are spread to form a canopy over the children and the oleh. This is followed by the calling up of the Chatan Torah, for whom the final verses of the Torah are read. After the completion of the reading, it is customary that Hagbaha is performed with arms crossed, so that when the Torah is raised and the arms uncrossed, the lettering on the scroll faces outward toward the congregation. A second scroll is opened; the Chatan Bereshit is called up and the first verses of Bereshit are read [Shulchan Aruch and Rema Orach Chaim 697:1]. It is customary to pause in the reading for the congregation to read aloud Veyehi-Erev Veyehi Voker for each day of Creation, and to read aloud the last three verses, starting with Veyechulu HaShamayim. This is followed by Half Kaddish. A third scroll is opened for Maftir. The Haftara is the beginning of the book of Joshua (page 1166) [ibid].
